focus.text: Pronouns are the words that save you from repeating a noun: *she*, *them*, *our*, *herself*, *everyone*. They keep writing short, but they only work when the reader can see at once which noun each one stands for. Two habits cause most of the trouble in Vietnamese students' essays: leaving out a subject that English insists on (*It is important…*), and adding a pronoun that English does not want (*My brother he plays football*). Choose the right form, point it at one clear noun, and a paragraph holds together by itself.

summaryTable.caption: What each kind of pronoun does
rows: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
me, you, him, her, it, us, them
my, your, his, her, its, our, their
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
**Everyone has** a copy of the plan.

pretest.sentence: My sister and I share a small room near the university.
pretest.reason: The pair is the subject of *share*, so the subject pronoun *I* is right.

pretest.sentence: My brother he works at a hotel in Nha Trang.
pretest.reason: *My brother* is already the subject, so the extra *he* has to go.

pretest.sentence: Is important to check your spelling before you submit.
pretest.reason: The sentence has no subject: write *It is important…*.

pretest.sentence: The manager gave us a schedule for the whole month.
pretest.reason: *Us* is the object pronoun after the verb *gave*.

pretest.sentence: Between you and I, the second plan is safer.
pretest.reason: *Between* is a preposition, so it takes the object pronoun *me*.

pretest.sentence: Linh cooked the whole meal herself.
pretest.reason: The reflexive *herself* stresses that Linh had no help.

pretest.sentence: My mother is a nurse, and he works at night.
pretest.reason: *Mother* is female, so the pronoun must be *she*.

pretest.sentence: Everyone in the group has to submit their own report.
pretest.reason: *Everyone* takes a singular verb, and *their* is standard when the person's gender is unknown.

pretest.sentence: Nobody in my class have visited Sa Pa.
pretest.reason: *Nobody* is singular, so the verb is *has*.

pretest.sentence: The council closed two bus routes last year, and this decision still angers commuters.
pretest.reason: *This decision* names what *this* refers to, so the reference is clear.

context.title: The stall outside the factory
context.paragraph: Khoa and his younger sister run a small stall that sells bánh mì outside a factory in Biên Hòa. They open at half past five, because the workers buy their breakfast on the way in. Khoa makes the sauce himself, and he says the recipe came from their grandmother. Customers often tell him that it tastes better than the version sold in the market. Last year the pair saved enough to buy a second cart, and that purchase doubled what they earn. It is not an easy job, and neither of them has much free time. Still, my father, who buys from them every Monday, says nobody works harder in the whole street.

sections.title: Forming personal, possessive and reflexive pronouns

table.caption: The full set of personal pronouns

notes: A possessive determiner is followed by a noun (*her essay*); a possessive pronoun stands alone (*the essay is hers*).
Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: *hers, ours, theirs, its*. *It's* always means *it is* or *it has*.

items.stem: The teacher asked Hùng and ___ to stay behind.
items.reason: The pair is the object of *asked*, so use *me*.

items.stem: This bag is not mine. I think it is ___.
items.reason: No noun follows, so the possessive pronoun *hers* is needed.

items.stem: My parents sold ___ old motorbike in June.
items.reason: A noun follows, so use the possessive determiner *their*.

items.stem: Trang and ___ travelled to Đà Lạt by coach.
items.reason: The pair is the subject of *travelled*, so use *I*.

items.stem: The committee published ___ report last Friday.

sections.title: Using pronouns: subjects, doubles and reflexives

rules.text: Every English sentence needs a subject, even when that subject carries no meaning of its own (*it*, *there*).

examples.text: **It** is difficult to find a quiet place to revise.
**There** are three bus stops within ten minutes of our school.

rules.text: Name the subject once. Do not follow a noun subject with a pronoun that repeats it.

examples.text: **My brother plays** football every Sunday morning.
**The students who joined late still passed** the course.
bold: The students who joined late still passed

rules.text: Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and the object are the same person or thing.

tips: *By myself* means alone. *Myself* on its own adds emphasis: *I ran the survey myself.* It is never a polite substitute for *I* or *me*.

sections.title: Using pronouns with a clear reference

rules.text: Check that each pronoun points back to one noun, and that it matches that noun in number and gender.

examples.text: My mother teaches maths, and **she** marks papers every evening.
The two reports arrived late, so the editor returned **them**.

rules.text: If a pronoun could point at two different nouns, repeat the noun instead of guessing.

examples.text: Mai told Huyền that **Huyền** had won the scholarship.
We compared the old syllabus with the new one, and **the new syllabus** had fewer topics.

rules.text: Keep the same person all the way through a paragraph; do not slide from *students* to *you*.

examples.text: **Students** who plan their week finish **their** essays on time.

items.sentence: My father he drives a taxi in Hải Phòng.
items.reason: *My father* is already the subject, so the extra pronoun has to go.

items.sentence: Is necessary to book the tickets a week early.
items.reason: The sentence has no subject; add the dummy subject *it*.

items.sentence: My grandmother lives in Huế, and he grows orchids on the roof.
items.reason: *Grandmother* is female, so the pronoun is *she*.

items.sentence: The book that I borrowed it is due on Friday.
items.reason: *That* already stands for the object, so *it* repeats it.

items.sentence: Nga and me organised the charity sale in October.
items.reason: The pair is the subject of *organised*, so use *I*.

sections.title: Forming sentences with indefinite pronouns

table.caption: Indefinite pronouns and the verb that follows them
rows: **Everyone has** a copy of the timetable.
each of, either of, neither of
**Each of the reports was** checked twice.
both of, several of, many of
some of, all of, most of
**Most of the water was** wasted. / **Most of the students were** late.

notes: *Each*, *every*, *either* and *neither* stay singular in formal writing, even when a plural noun comes between them and the verb.

sections.title: Using indefinite pronouns and avoiding vague this and it

rules.text: Indefinite pronouns ending in *-one*, *-body* or *-thing* take a singular verb, whatever noun comes after them.

examples.text: **Everyone** in the two groups **has** signed the form.

rules.text: To refer back to an indefinite pronoun, *they* and *their* are normal in modern writing when the person's gender is unknown.

examples.text: If **anyone** wants a copy, **they** can email the office.
**Somebody** has left **their** umbrella in the hall.

rules.text: *Each of*, *one of* and *neither of* stay singular, even though a plural noun follows *of*.

examples.text: **Each of the districts has** its own recycling scheme.
**Neither of the plans was** cheap enough.

rules.text: Do not let *this*, *that* or *it* point at a whole paragraph. Add a noun that names the idea.

examples.text: Ticket prices rose twice in one year. **This increase** pushed commuters back onto motorbikes.
Two teachers left in March. **That change** slowed the project down.

tips: When you start a sentence with *This*, ask yourself *this what?* If you cannot answer in one noun, your reader cannot either.

items.stem: Everyone in the two teams ___ received a certificate.
items.reason: *Everyone* is singular, so the auxiliary is *has*.

items.stem: Neither of the two proposals ___ realistic, so the committee rejected both.
items.reason: *Neither of* takes a singular verb, and the sentence is in the past.

items.stem: One of my classmates ___ to school by ferry.
items.reason: The subject is *one*, not *classmates*, so the verb takes -s.

items.stem: Somebody has left ___ helmet on the stairs.
items.reason: *Their* is the possessive form and is standard after an indefinite pronoun.

items.stem: The volunteers painted the whole classroom ___.
items.reason: The subject and the object are the same people, so use the reflexive *themselves*.

editing.text: Last summer my cousin Đạt and me worked at a homestay in Mộc Châu. The owner, Mrs Liên, trained us for two days, and then she left us to run the kitchen by ourself. Is not easy to cook for twenty guests. My cousin he is better at planning than I am, so he wrote the menus and I did the shopping. One morning a guest asked us for a vegetarian dish, and we made her a tofu salad. She said it was the best meal of hers stay. Everyone in the two families were happy with the food that week. My aunt owns homestay next door, and he told Mrs Liên that our salad was becoming famous. That was the summer I learned to trust me in a kitchen.

errors.reason: The pair is the subject of *worked*, so use *I*.
*We* is plural, so the reflexive is *ourselves*.
The sentence has no subject; add the dummy subject *it*.
*My cousin* is already the subject, so the extra pronoun has to go.
*Hers* stands alone; before a noun the form is *her*.
The subject is *everyone*, which is singular, so the verb is *was*.
*Next door* tells the reader which homestay, so it takes *the*.
*My aunt* is female, so the pronoun is *she*.
The subject *I* and the object are the same person, so use *myself*.

topics.prompt: Write an email to a friend describing a group project you and two classmates finished last term. Say who did what and what you would do differently next time.
checklist: Subject and object pronouns are in the right form (*Minh and I planned…*, *the teacher thanked us*).
No noun subject is repeated by a pronoun (*my partner he…*).
At least one reflexive pronoun shows that somebody did something without help.

topics.prompt: "Social media makes it harder for teenagers to concentrate." Give your opinion with two reasons and one example from your own week.
checklist: Every sentence has a subject, including the ones that begin with *It is…* or *There are…*.
Indefinite pronouns (*everyone*, *nobody*, *each of*) take singular verbs.
*This* and *it* are followed by a noun whenever they refer back to a whole idea.

topics.prompt: Report on a small survey your class carried out about how students travel to school. Describe who took part and what the results showed.
checklist: Each pronoun points clearly at one noun; the noun is repeated where a pronoun would be ambiguous.
*Each of*, *one of* and *neither of* take singular verbs.
Possessive determiners (*their answers*) and possessive pronouns (*the longest was theirs*) are each used in the right place.
